sections.h2: Who records deeds in Santa Cruz County, Arizona?
sections.html:
The Santa Cruz County Recorder records deeds, mortgages, maps and surveys for the whole county, and the same office keeps voter registration records. Every document the office accepts gets a docket and page number, is indexed and is microfilmed. Searchable documents on the county’s Recorder page start with 1984. For questions, call 520-375-7990 or email recorder@santacruzcountyaz.gov.

The county sits on the Mexican border, and it is the smallest county in Arizona by area. Nogales is the county seat. Rio Rico, Tubac, Sonoita and Patagonia all record at the same office, so a deed for a house in any of them follows the same rules. The county was formed in 1899 out of Pima County.

sections.h2: What must a deed look like before the Recorder will accept it?
sections.html:
Arizona sets the format in ARS 11-480, and an instrument that misses one of the listed conditions may be rejected on the spot. Check these before you send anything.

  • A caption that names the document, such as warranty deed or release of mortgage.
  • An original, legible instrument with original signatures unless the law says otherwise.
  • Page size no larger than 8.5 by 14 inches and type no smaller than ten point, for documents signed on or after January 1, 1991.
  • A half-inch margin on all sides and a top margin of at least two inches on the first page, which the Recorder reserves for recording stamps.
  • If the instrument changes an earlier recorded document, the earlier document’s recording date, docket and page.

The Recorder’s page points to the same statute and also to the exemption codes in ARS 11-1134. Return-to information may go in the left three and one-half inches of the first page’s top margin.

sections.h2: What is the affidavit of legal value, and when is a deed exempt?
sections.html:
Each deed that transfers title, and each sales contract, needs an affidavit of legal value signed by the buyer and seller or their agent. Under ARS 11-1133 it states names and addresses, the legal description, the parcel number, the sale date, the total consideration and type of financing, whether personal property is five percent or more of the price, and for a house, whether it will be owner-occupied or rented. The Recorder must refuse to record a deed without a complete affidavit unless the instrument carries a notation of an exemption.

The exemption list in ARS 11-1134 covers many family and entity transfers. Examples are a deed of gift, a conveyance under a court order, a quitclaim deed for no monetary consideration, a trustee’s deed under a power of sale, a deed that corrects an earlier one, and transfers of residential property for nominal consideration between spouses, parents and children, grandparents and grandchildren, or siblings. The instrument must note the specific exemption on its face at recording. Ask the title company which one applies.

sections.h2: How much does recording a deed cost in Santa Cruz County?
sections.html:
The statutory fee is $30 per instrument, or $15 when the United States, Arizona or a political subdivision is a party and requests the recording. The county fee schedule below covers the other charges the Recorder lists. The Recorder’s page also links a 2026 fee sheet, so ask the office to confirm the current amounts before you send payment.

Recording a standard instrument$30 per instrumentARS 11-475
Instrument with a government party$15ARS 11-475
Copies$1 per pageCounty fee schedule
Certification of copies$3.00 plus $1.00 per pageCounty fee schedule

Requests for copies go to the Recorder in writing by email with advance payment. A map no larger than 8.5 by 14 inches can be recorded as a standard document, and the standard fee applies.

sections.h2: Does Santa Cruz County charge a transfer tax on a home sale?
sections.html:
State law sets a flat real estate transfer fee of $2 per deed or contract, and the recorder collects it before recording. Under ARS 11-1132 that $2 is already part of the $30 standard recording fee, so it does not add to the total. A county may also add a special recording surcharge of up to $4 per instrument for its document storage system, and that amount is likewise included in the $30.

The statute defines "value" for the affidavit as the full actual consideration paid or to be paid, including any liens. In a gift or a deed with nominal consideration, it is the estimated price the property would bring on the open market. Ask the Recorder or your title company to confirm whether any other charge applies to your deed.

sections.h2: Do I need photo ID to record a deed in person?
sections.html:
Yes, for most in-person filers. ARS 11-472 requires valid photo identification for any document recorded in person at the Recorder’s office or a recording kiosk, and the county notice says the requirement took effect September 11, 2026. Accepted IDs for individuals include a driver’s license or state ID, a passport or passport card, a U.S. military ID and a tribal ID.

The statute exempts documents submitted by an escrow officer or office, a title insurance agent or insurer, a state or federally chartered bank or credit union, an active member of the State Bar of Arizona and a governmental entity. Exempt filers on the county’s list show items such as a bar card with a government ID, an employee badge or a company letter. The Recorder notes the type of ID, the name and the number, but keeps no copy, and that information is not a public record.

sections.h2: How do I pay the Santa Cruz County Recorder?
sections.html:
The office takes card payments in person or by phone, 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., Monday through Friday, Arizona time. Payments from $0 to $60 carry a flat $1.50 surcharge on Visa, Mastercard and Discover credit cards. Visa Signature Debit carries a flat $3.95 surcharge. Payments of $61 and up carry a 2.49 percent surcharge. The Recorder does not keep the surcharge.

For context on the local housing stock, the Census Bureau counts 20,135 housing units, a 69.3 percent owner-occupied rate and a median owner-occupied value of $233,000 for 2020 to 2024, per Census QuickFacts.

sections.h2: What should a seller in Santa Cruz County know about recording?
sections.html:
• Confirm the deed carries a caption, an original signature and the two-inch top margin.
  • Sign the affidavit of legal value or note an exemption on the face of the deed.
  • Let the title or escrow company file, since they are exempt from the in-person ID rule.
  • Ask the Recorder for the 2026 fee sheet, and the Treasurer for any tax balance, before closing.

If the buyer is a company, ask who will present the deed. The Recorder’s staff can explain the format rules, though they cannot give legal advice.

faqs.q: How much does it cost to record a deed in Santa Cruz County?
faqs.a: The statutory fee is $30 per instrument, or $15 for instruments to which the United States, Arizona or a political subdivision is a party. Copies cost $1 per page and certification adds $3 plus $1 per page. Ask the Recorder to confirm the 2026 fee sheet.

faqs.q: Is there a transfer tax in Santa Cruz County?
faqs.a: Arizona sets a flat $2 real estate transfer fee per deed or contract, and it is included in the $30 recording fee. Ask the Recorder or your title company whether any other charge applies to your deed.

faqs.q: Do I need an affidavit of legal value to record a deed?
faqs.a: Usually yes. A deed or sales contract must carry a completed affidavit signed by buyer and seller or their agents, unless the instrument notes an exemption under ARS 11-1134, such as a deed of gift or a court-ordered conveyance.

faqs.q: Who is exempt from the photo ID rule for in-person recording?
faqs.a: Escrow officers and offices, title insurance agents and insurers, state or federally chartered banks and credit unions, active State Bar of Arizona members and government entities. Everyone else who records in person must show valid photo ID.

faqs.q: How do I reach the Santa Cruz County Recorder?
faqs.a: Call 520-375-7990 or email recorder@santacruzcountyaz.gov. Card payments by phone are taken from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., Monday through Friday. Searchable recorded documents begin with 1984.
